messages.content: You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
whats the easiest sundew for a total beginner

Drosera capensis, the Cape sundew, is the one almost everyone starts with. It is subtropical, so it grows all year and never needs a dormancy period, and it shrugs off the usual beginner mistakes as long as you keep it in bright light and standing water. Give it a 1:1 mix of sphagnum peat and perlite, water only with distilled or rainwater, and it will be dewy within a few weeks. It also self-seeds so freely that you will end up giving plants away.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How much light does a sundew actually need? I keep reading "bright" but that means nothing to me.

Aim for at least 4 to 6 hours of direct sun, or 12 to 14 hours a day under a decent LED. A south-facing window in the northern hemisphere is usually the best spot indoors, and outdoors full sun is ideal for most species. The practical test is the plant itself: strong light produces short, compact, heavily dewed leaves with red tentacles, while weak light produces long floppy green leaves with little or no dew.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Why isn't it sticky?

Loss of dew is nearly always one of three things: not enough light, air that is too dry, or recent disturbance like repotting or shipping. Move it to your brightest window or put it 6 to 10 inches under a grow light, keep the soil wet by standing the pot in a tray, and stop any fan or heating vent from blowing across it. Do not judge the old leaves - watch for the new leaves that unfurl over the next two to three weeks, because those coming in glistening is the real sign that the plant is happy.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
My sundew arrived totally dry and sad looking. Did I get scammed?

Almost certainly not - sundews routinely lose all their dew in transit because of the dark box and the dry air, and it looks alarming. Pot it up in peat and perlite, stand it in a tray of distilled water, and put it somewhere very bright, then leave it alone. Dew usually returns on existing leaves in one to two weeks, and the first new leaf to emerge already sparkling is your confirmation that it has settled in.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
I have a D. capensis under a south window and the new leaves have no dew. Old leaves still have some. What am I doing wrong?

If new growth is coming in dry while the old leaves still hold dew, the plant is usually reacting to dry indoor air or air movement rather than to light. Check whether a heating or AC vent blows anywhere near it, since a steady draft evaporates the mucilage faster than the plant can produce it. Keeping the pot in a water tray raises the humidity right around the leaves, and grouping it with other plants or using a shallow gravel-and-water tray around the pot helps too. If your window has a low sun angle in winter, adding a small LED for 12 hours will also make a visible difference.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
do sundews need a humidifier

Not usually. Most sundews, D. capensis especially, do fine at ordinary household humidity of 40 to 50 percent as long as the soil stays wet, because the tray of water under the pot creates a moister pocket of air right at leaf level. Humidity only becomes a real problem in a dry winter house running forced-air heat, where levels can drop under 30 percent. In that case a small humidifier nearby, or a clear dome for a couple of weeks while a new plant establishes, will bring the dew back.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Explain the tray method

Stand the pot in a saucer or tray and keep roughly 1 to 2 cm of distilled, RO, or rainwater in it at all times, letting the peat wick moisture up from below. Sundews are bog plants and want the soil constantly wet, so unlike most houseplants they should never be allowed to dry out. Top the tray back up whenever it runs dry rather than letting it sit empty for days. In very hot weather you may need to refill daily; in winter every few days is plenty.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Can I use bottled spring water?

No - spring water carries dissolved minerals just like tap water, and those salts build up in the peat and burn the roots over a few months. Stick to distilled water, reverse osmosis water, or collected rainwater, all of which are effectively mineral-free. If you want to check a water source, a cheap TDS meter is worth the money; under 50 ppm is acceptable and under 10 ppm is ideal. Never use tap water, softened water, or filtered pitcher water.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
what soil mix do sundews want

A nutrient-free mix, most simply 1 part sphagnum peat moss to 1 part perlite or silica sand by volume. Live or long-fibered sphagnum works well on its own too, especially for species like D. adelae. What matters is that there is no fertilizer, no lime, no compost, and no bark or standard potting soil in it, because nutrients in the soil will kill the roots. Rinse perlite and sand before mixing, and check that any peat you buy has no added wetting agents or fertilizer.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Should I be feeding my sundew or will it feed itself?

Indoors a healthy sundew catches plenty on its own, particularly fungus gnats, so feeding is genuinely optional. If you want to speed up growth, put a small insect or a pinch of rehydrated dried bloodworms on one or two tentacled leaves every couple of weeks. Keep the portion tiny - roughly the size of the sticky pad on the leaf - because oversized food rots and can kill the leaf. Never put fertilizer in the soil as a shortcut.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
I bought a sundew specifically to deal with fungus gnats. Does that actually work?

It works better than you would expect. A mature D. capensis or D. spatulata will paper itself in gnats within days of an outbreak, since gnats are exactly the small weak fliers the dew is built to catch. Place the plant right next to whichever houseplant is producing the gnats, because the sundew has to be in their flight path to intercept them. It will not eliminate larvae in the other pot's soil, so pair it with letting that soil dry out between waterings.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
leaf is slowly wrapping around a fly, is my plant dying

That is completely normal and a sign of a healthy, well-fed plant. Sundew leaves bend the tentacles and often the whole lamina around captured prey over several hours to a couple of days, which pushes more digestive glands into contact with the meal. Once digestion finishes, in roughly a week, the leaf unrolls again and the dry husk stays stuck on. Leave it alone while it is curled - poking at it just wastes the plant's energy.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Which sundews need a dormancy and which ones don't? I want to avoid the ones that do.

Subtropical and tropical species need no dormancy at all - D. capensis, D. spatulata, D. aliciae, and D. adelae just keep growing year round on a windowsill. Temperate species do require a cold winter rest: D. rotundifolia, D. filiformis, D. intermedia, and D. anglica all form a tight resting bud called a hibernaculum and need several months of cold. If you want to avoid the whole issue, buy any of the first group; the Cape sundew is the obvious pick.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
whats a hibernaculum

It is the tight winter resting bud that temperate sundews form as day length and temperature drop in autumn. The plant pulls its energy into a small knot of curled, dew-free leaves at the crown, the old foliage dies back and browns, and the whole thing sits dormant for about three to four months. Keep the soil damp and cold, around 1 to 10 degrees Celsius, and do not throw the pot out thinking it died. It will unfurl into new growth in spring on its own.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How do I overwinter a D. filiformis in a zone where it freezes?

In most of its hardy range you can simply leave the pot outside, since D. filiformis is temperate and wants that cold. Mulch around the pot with pine needles or sink it into the ground so the roots do not freeze solid in a small container, and keep the soil damp but not sitting in a deep tray of ice. It will die back to a hibernaculum for roughly three to four months and push new threadlike leaves in spring. If you cannot leave it outdoors, an unheated garage or a bagged pot in the fridge at 2 to 5 degrees Celsius for three months works.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Is D. rotundifolia a good indoor plant?

Not really, because it is temperate and needs a genuine cold winter rest with a hibernaculum, which is awkward to arrange in a warm house. It grows beautifully outdoors in a bog pot in full sun in temperate climates, where the seasons handle dormancy for you. Kept warm and lit year round it will usually decline and die within a year or two. For an indoor plant choose a subtropical like D. capensis or D. aliciae instead.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
tell me about growing D. binata

The forked sundew is vigorous and gets large, with Y-shaped or repeatedly branched leaves that can reach 20 to 30 cm. It wants the same wet peat and perlite, mineral-free water, and very bright light as the rest, and it does best with full sun. Most forms benefit from a cool winter rest with shorter days, during which the foliage may die back entirely, and it regrows from its thick roots in spring. Those thick roots also make it one of the best candidates for root cuttings.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
my D. adelae is in a dim corner and looks ok, can it stay there?

D. adelae tolerates less intense light than most sundews and it is the species people succeed with in terrariums, but a dim corner still starves it. It wants bright indirect light or gentle direct sun, and under proper light the leaves flush deep red and the dew is heavy; in low light it goes plain green and stops producing much mucilage. It is tropical, so no dormancy, and it likes warmth and higher humidity than average. Move it somewhere brighter and it will spread by root runners into a clump.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Difference between D. spatulata and D. aliciae? They look similar in photos.

Both are small rosetted subtropical species, easy, and neither needs dormancy. D. spatulata has spoon-shaped leaves on a flatter, looser rosette and is famous for seeding itself into every neighboring pot. D. aliciae forms a tighter, more symmetrical wedge-leaved rosette that flushes red in strong sun and tends to stay as a neater single plant. Care is identical for both: wet peat and perlite, distilled water, and as much light as you can give them.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How do I take a leaf cutting?

Cut a healthy, actively growing leaf off near the base with clean scissors, then either lay it flat on damp sphagnum or float it face up on 1 cm of distilled water in a covered container. Put it somewhere bright but not scorching, and keep it humid by covering with a lid or clear bag. Plantlets typically appear along the leaf within three to six weeks, and once they have a couple of leaves and visible roots you can pot them into standard peat and perlite mix. D. capensis is almost absurdly reliable this way.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
do root cuttings work on sundews

They work well on species with thick fleshy roots, which mainly means D. capensis, D. binata, and D. adelae. Cut healthy root sections about 2 to 5 cm long, lay them horizontally on damp peat or sphagnum, barely cover them, and keep them humid and bright. New plantlets push up from the root pieces in roughly four to eight weeks. It is a good way to use the roots you break off during repotting instead of throwing them away.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
I keep finding baby sundews in my other pots. Where are they coming from?

That is D. capensis or D. spatulata self-seeding, and it is completely normal. Both are self-fertile, so their flowers set seed without any pollinator, the capsules split, and the dust-fine seed drifts into every pot on the same tray. If you like the free plants, just leave them; if you do not want them, snip the flower stalks off before the capsules ripen. Seedlings reach a decent size in about six to twelve months.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
my capensis is sending up a flower stalk. Should I cut it?

That depends on what you want. Flowering costs the plant some energy and can briefly slow leaf production, so cutting the stalk at the base keeps growth focused on foliage. If you want seed, leave it - D. capensis is self-fertile, the small pink flowers open one at a time in the morning, and each spent flower forms a capsule of fine seed a few weeks later. Either choice is safe for the plant.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How do I collect sundew seed?

Wait until the flower stalk has dried and the capsules have turned brown and started to split, usually three to five weeks after the flowers finish. Snip the whole stalk off over a sheet of paper and tap or crush the capsules gently - the seed is like black dust, so work somewhere without a draft. Store it dry in a paper envelope somewhere cool; subtropical species stay viable for a year or two. Temperate species like D. rotundifolia and D. filiformis need a few weeks of cold moist stratification before they will germinate.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
how do i sow the seed

Sprinkle it on the surface of wet peat and perlite and do not bury it, since sundew seed needs light to germinate. Stand the pot in a tray of distilled water, cover with a clear lid or bag to hold humidity, and keep it bright and warm at around 20 to 25 degrees Celsius. Subtropical species usually sprout in two to six weeks; temperate ones need cold stratification first and can take longer. The seedlings are tiny specks at first, so be patient and resist the urge to disturb the surface.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Can I divide a big clumping sundew?

Yes, for species that naturally form clumps or offsets, such as D. adelae, D. binata, and older D. capensis that have grown multiple crowns. Tip the plant out, tease the root mass apart by hand into pieces that each carry a crown and some roots, and pot them separately into fresh peat and perlite. Do this in the growing season, keep them wet, and expect them to sulk and lose dew for a week or two before new leaves come in. Broken root fragments left behind will often sprout into extra plants.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
When and how should I repot a sundew?

Every one to two years is plenty, mainly to refresh the peat before it breaks down and turns sour. Spring or early summer is the best timing for subtropicals, and for temperate species do it in late winter while they are still in hibernaculum. Slide the root ball out, shake off most of the old mix, and set the plant into fresh 1:1 peat and perlite with the crown right at soil level. Expect a temporary loss of dew afterwards - it is disturbance, not damage, and new dewy leaves in two to three weeks means it recovered.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Sundew has more dew in the morning than the afternoon. Normal?

Yes, that daily rhythm is completely normal. Mucilage production peaks overnight and in the cool humid morning, then evaporates back during the hottest, driest part of the day, so an afternoon plant often looks less spectacular than the same plant at 8am. Plants outdoors in wind or hot sun show this most strongly. As long as dew rebuilds by the next morning and new leaves emerge sticky, there is nothing to fix.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
i touched it and now my finger is sticky and it wont wash off easily

That is just the mucilage, and it is harmless - it is mostly water and polysaccharides, not glue or acid. Warm soapy water and a bit of rubbing takes it off; plain cold water alone tends to smear it around. On the plant side, one poke costs it a few tentacles' worth of dew that will regenerate in a day or so, so try not to make a habit of it. The plant is not damaged by being touched.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
can i rinse dust off my sundew

Yes, but do it with distilled, RO, or rainwater, never from the tap, and use a gentle spray or a slow trickle rather than a hard stream. The rinse will wash the dew off, which looks dramatic, but a healthy plant in good light regenerates it within roughly 24 hours. It is a reasonable way to clear dust, aphids, or a mess of dead insects. Do not use soap, insecticidal spray, or leaf shine on a carnivorous plant.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
The bottom leaves keep turning black and dying. Is it rot?

If it is only the oldest, lowest leaves while the center keeps pushing new growth, that is just normal turnover - sundew leaves have a lifespan of a couple of months and are constantly replaced. Dead ones darken, dry up, and stay attached, which looks worse than it is. You can trim them off with scissors for tidiness, or leave them; neither harms the plant. Worry only if the crown itself goes soft and mushy or if new leaves are the ones dying.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
brown crispy tips on the leaves of my capensis

Brown tips usually mean the tip dried out, most often from low humidity, a draft, or the plant burning through an oversized insect that rotted on the leaf. Mineral-contaminated water is the other common cause, so double-check that nothing but distilled, RO, or rainwater is going into the tray. Keep the soil wet, move it away from vents and fans, and feed smaller portions. New leaves coming in clean means you fixed it; the old damaged tips will not heal and can be trimmed.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Does a sundew need a terrarium?

No. Subtropical species like D. capensis, D. spatulata, and D. aliciae grow perfectly well in the open on a sunny windowsill and generally prefer the airflow. Terrariums suit the humidity-loving tropicals better, D. adelae in particular, and they are useful as a temporary recovery chamber for a newly shipped or freshly repotted plant. If you do use one, remember that glass cuts light, so you will almost always need a grow light over it. Watch for mold in a sealed enclosure with no air exchange.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Best window for a sundew in the northern hemisphere?

South-facing gives the most hours of direct sun and is the first choice, with west-facing a decent second. Put the pot right against the glass rather than a metre back, because light intensity falls off fast with distance. If the only option is an east or north window, plan on supplementing with an LED for 12 to 14 hours a day. Watch that the glass does not cook the plant on hot afternoons - the tray of water helps buffer that.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
What grow light specs should I use for sundews? I'm setting up a shelf.

A basic full-spectrum LED bar or panel run 12 to 14 hours a day on a timer is all you need. Hang it so the plants sit roughly 15 to 30 cm below it, which for most hobby LEDs lands somewhere near 200 to 400 micromoles of PPFD - plenty for compact, red, dewy growth. Start further away and lower the light over a week or two so the plant acclimates without bleaching. Keep the tray topped up, since lights dry the air and the tray water faster than a windowsill does.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
I have a small fan for air circulation in my plant shelf and my sundew looks bare

Point the fan somewhere else. A fan blowing directly across a sundew evaporates the mucilage as fast as the plant secretes it, and the plant will read as permanently dew-free even in perfect light. Gentle indirect circulation in the room is fine and even helpful against mold, but the airflow should not be aimed at the leaves. Once the draft stops, dew typically rebuilds within a few days.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Can I give it a tiny bit of diluted fertilizer to speed it up?

Not in the soil - sundew roots are adapted to nutrient-free bog peat and will burn, and root damage often kills the plant outright. The nutrients they want come in through the leaves, from insects. If you want to push growth, feed prey or rehydrated dried bloodworms on the leaves every couple of weeks instead. Experienced growers do use very dilute foliar sprays, but it is easy to overdo and there is no reason for a beginner to risk it.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
I put a mealworm on my sundew and now the leaf is going black. What happened?

The food was too big. A leaf can only digest what its glands can fully cover, and anything larger sits there and rots, taking the leaf with it. Pull the remains off, and the plant will simply replace that leaf - it is not a whole-plant emergency. Next time use something the size of a fruit fly, or a pinch of rehydrated bloodworms roughly matching the sticky area, and stick to one or two leaves at a time.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
how do you feed bloodworms exactly

Take a few freeze-dried bloodworms, drop them in a small amount of distilled water for about 5 minutes until they soften, then mash them into a paste. Use a toothpick or tweezers to place a portion about the size of a match head onto the dewy part of a healthy leaf, making sure it contacts the mucilage rather than sliding off. Feed one to three leaves every two weeks or so during the growing season. Do not let paste fall onto the soil, since it adds nutrients where you do not want them.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
What kind of pot should I use?

Plastic, glazed ceramic, or polystyrene - anything inert. Avoid terracotta and unglazed clay, because they leach minerals into the mix and wick salts to the surface. Depth matters more than width for most sundews, since even small rosettes send roots surprisingly deep, so a pot 10 to 13 cm tall is a good default and D. capensis appreciates more. Make sure it has drainage holes so the tray can wick water up.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Do I need to change anything for my capensis in winter?

It needs no dormancy, so the routine stays the same, but the conditions around it change. Days are shorter and duller, so either move it to the brightest window or add an LED on a 12 to 14 hour timer, and expect somewhat slower growth regardless. Indoor heating dries the air, which is the usual reason people lose dew in January, so keep the tray full and move it away from radiators and vents. Water use drops, so check the tray every few days rather than daily.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
repotted my sundew a week ago and now it looks flat and dewless, did i kill it

Almost certainly not - that is the standard post-repot sulk. Disturbing the roots interrupts water transport, and the plant drops its dew and goes limp while it re-establishes. Keep it wet in a tray, keep it bright, resist fiddling with it, and optionally bag it loosely for a week to hold humidity. Watch the crown: a new leaf unfurling with dew, usually within two to three weeks, means it made it.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Will my sundew starve if it never catches anything?

No. Sundews photosynthesize like any plant, and insects are a nutrient supplement that lets them grow faster and larger in soil with almost nothing in it. A plant that catches nothing for months will survive, it will just be smaller and slower. Indoors this rarely comes up anyway, since fungus gnats and stray fruit flies find them on their own. Feeding by hand every couple of weeks is a boost, not a requirement.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
There's white fuzzy mold growing on the dead bugs stuck to my plant. Should I panic?

No, but improve the air. Mold on prey remains usually means stagnant, very humid air, often in a closed terrarium or under a dome, and it typically stays on the dead insect rather than attacking healthy tissue. Pick the mouldy leaf or the affected prey off, open up the enclosure, and add gentle indirect air movement in the room. If mold is spreading onto the crown or into the soil, get the plant out of the enclosure entirely and cut back on hand-feeding.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Cheapest way to get water for these plants long-term?

Collecting rainwater is the cheapest by far - a clean bin or barrel under a downspout will cover a whole collection for free. Distilled water by the jug from a grocery store is the simplest for one or two plants, running a few dollars a week at most. If you keep a lot of plants, a countertop reverse osmosis unit pays for itself within a year. Whatever you use, keep the TDS under about 50 ppm and never fall back on tap water in a pinch.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
My sundew is turning red. Is it stressed or dying?

Red is a good sign in almost every case - the anthocyanin pigments develop in response to strong light, and species like D. aliciae, D. spatulata, and D. capensis "Red Form" go deep red or maroon in full sun. Combine that red with heavy dew and compact leaves and you have a plant getting exactly what it wants. What you want to avoid is the opposite: pale, stretched, green, dew-free leaves, which mean too little light. Only worry about redness if it comes with wilting or blackening tissue.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
The water in my sundew tray goes green and slimy in summer. Is that bad for the plant?

Algae in the tray is ugly but harmless to the plant itself. It grows because sunlight hits standing water; using an opaque tray, or one that is shaded by the pots, largely stops it. Rinse the tray out with plain distilled water every week or two in hot weather and refill, and do not use algaecide or bleach anywhere near a carnivorous plant. If the surface of the peat itself is greening over, that just means it is very wet and bright, which sundews tolerate fine.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Is it safe to move my sundew outside for the summer?

Yes, and most species grow dramatically better outdoors in full sun. Acclimate it over a week or two by starting in partial shade and increasing exposure, or the leaves will scorch after months of weak indoor light. Keep it in a tray of rainwater and expect to top it up daily in heat. Bring subtropicals like D. capensis back in before frost, since they get no dormancy and will not survive a freeze; temperate species can stay out.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
what's the fastest way to get more capensis plants for free

Leaf cuttings and seed, and both are trivially easy with this species. Float two or three healthy leaves on distilled water in a covered takeaway tub under bright light and you will see plantlets in three to six weeks. At the same time let one flower stalk mature - it self-pollinates without any help and gives you hundreds of seeds you can scatter on wet peat. Between the two you can go from one plant to a full tray inside a year.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
i think my sundew is dying. leaves have no dew, some are brown, but there is a tiny curled thing in the middle. it lives outside.

If it is autumn and this is a temperate species like D. rotundifolia, D. filiformis, D. intermedia, or D. anglica, that tiny curled thing in the middle is a hibernaculum and the plant is going dormant exactly as it should. Leave it outside, keep the soil damp and cold, and do not bring it into a warm room to "save" it. It will sit like that for roughly three to four months and then unfurl new dewy leaves in spring. If it is a subtropical species and it is not autumn, then the same symptoms point instead to too little light or a draft.
